item.title: QE ArXiv Watch: Week of September 28 - October 05, 2026
item.description:
The most quietly radical idea this week: stop pretending your estimator is smooth and your measurement plan is “information-matrix optimal.”

If you’re selecting sensors, test points, pixels, or inspections because downstream you’ll run Lasso / elastic net / TV denoising, then classical A- and D-optimality can be aiming at the wrong target. Marques et al. basically say: design for what you actually deploy, not for a Gaussian-linear fairy tale.

Designing measurements for nonsmooth reality (and doing it without pain)

Marques et al. tackle a practitioner-shaped problem: we want a small subset of measurements, but our inference pipeline is nonsmooth. In that world, “maximize det(Fisher info)” can be like optimizing a car for top speed when you’re actually driving in snow.

Their move is bilevel experimental design: the lower level solves the exact nonsmooth estimator you’ll use; the upper level chooses which measurements to buy by minimizing a validation-style prediction risk—without needing ground-truth signals. Sparsity comes from continuous acquisition weights in [0,1]^M plus a concave “price” penalty, and they trace the whole budget–performance frontier via a price homotopy (multiple usable designs per run, not one design per budget).

What’s nice for us: they avoid the usual “differentiate through an argmin that’s nonsmooth” trap with a value-function penalty and a single-loop proximal-gradient method, with an O(1/K) stationarity guarantee under reasonable conditions.

The results are the kind that matter when budgets are tight: in sparse regression with <40 sensors, median test NMSE drops ~40% versus D-/A-optimal; in Fashion-MNIST pixel selection with ≤32 pixels, they beat every baseline in every paired comparison—massively. At high budgets they converge toward “random is fine,” which is also useful guidance: don’t over-engineer when you’ve already bought plenty of signal.

Zero-label “design,” but for eliciting priors from an LLM

Teng et al. isn’t DOE in the traditional sense, but the vibe is familiar: choose a small set of queries to efficiently learn a response surface. MARS builds a tabular classifier with zero task labels by asking an LLM for feature-level log-odds at representative “anchor” values (quantiles/categories), then interpolating into per-feature response functions. After that, prediction is just an additive score—no test-time LLM calls.

If you’re doing quality triage with weak/no labels and you can articulate domain priors in language (“higher vibration RMS strongly increases failure odds after X”), MARS is an intriguing bridge. It’s also refreshingly cost-aware: reported API spend is ~10% of a heavier baseline, with modest gains from repeated elicitation (R=1→5).

Reliability: the claim is the product

Two reliability papers land the same punch from different angles: reliability isn’t a number, it’s a statement with assumptions.

Hardy et al. show why “just add more tasks” doesn’t necessarily fix agent benchmark noise. Using Generalizability Theory with Bayesian mixed models, they separate what you think you’re measuring (model quality) from what you’re often measuring (model+scaffold system quality). System ranking reliability is very high; underlying-model ranking reliability can be awful—and scaffold choice can reorder models. The practical takeaway for anyone running internal leaderboards: if your evaluation pipeline (prompting/tooling/scaffold) varies, you may be ranking your harness more than your model. Also: pooling diverse benchmarks can buy more reliability per dollar than deepening one benchmark.

Boland et al. make the analogous point for power-system adequacy: expected unserved energy (USE) misses tail risk when renewables correlate. They propose a modular “metric factory” (transform + time aggregation + risk functional) that produces interpretable standards like CVaR of USE, tail probability of max outage, outage duration distributions, etc. If you manage reliability risk, you want more than one lens—especially one that can see the tail.

Pan et al. zoom out and argue for an AI reliability engineering program built around a “reliability triangle”: failure definition, operational envelope, and evidence. The useful bit for QE folks is how classical tools map over: exposure-adjusted recurrent-event models (don’t rank by raw counts), overdispersion handling, accelerated/adversarial testing framed as reliability growth, and controls aligned to where failures live (component vs operational loop vs agentic conduct vs governance).

One question to sit with

Across sensors, benchmarks, grids, and agents, the trend is the same: optimize and report against the thing you actually claim—not the convenient proxy.

So: in your world, what’s the proxy you’ve been optimizing because it was easy to compute—and what would change if you optimized the deployed decision rule instead?

Featured Papers This Week

  • Marques et al.: Sparse Experimental Design for Nonsmooth Estimators via Bilevel Optimization (Experimental Design)
  • Teng et al.: Marginal Response Surface Elicitation for Zero-Label Tabular Learning (Experimental Design)
  • Hardy et al.: Agent Evaluation Reliability: More Tasks Won't (Always) Fix An Agent Leaderboard (Reliability)
  • Boland et al.: Measures of Reliability Risk for the Australian Energy Sector (Reliability)
  • Pan et al.: Reliability Engineering for AI Systems: Challenges, Methods, and Directions (Reliability)
